Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I have to be on guard all the time

vignette: Six months ago, in a dust-choked valley outside a forward operating base, the world split into sound and smoke. One moment they were moving through a dry wash; the next, an explosion threw him against a rock wall. When the ringing finally faded into an unnerving quiet, he realized the comms were dead. No voices, just the hollow silence pressing against his helmet. He tried to crawl forward, but his lungs burned, dragging in hot, thin air that never seemed to reach the bottom of his chest. Before he could process it, figures emerged from the dust, weapons raised, and the violence that followed was close enough to taste-metallic, immediate, and relentless. He fought through it, but the memory would not hold together. Now, in the fluorescent hum of the university hospital where he works as a physician, Andre knows the event in fractured flashes: a scuff of boots on gravel, the sharp intake of his own breath, a silhouette that dissolves before he can name it. There are whole hours that simply vanish, leaving him to wonder who was there and what he actually did. The fragmented flashes do not follow a timeline. They arrive unbidden during charting, a boot print on cracked earth one minute, a swallowed shout the next, with no connective tissue between them. He knows the gaps will not fill, and he stops trying to reconstruct the afternoon altogether, pushing the images away the moment they surface. The hospital, which once felt like a place of order and purpose, has become a landscape of potential threats. Andre scans every room as he enters, his shoulders locked, his eyes tracking exits and doorways. He has come to believe that the safety he once took for granted is an illusion; the world is unpredictable, and his old assumptions about how people operate have completely unraveled. The person who used to feel sure of his path doesn't exist anymore. He looks in the mirror and sees a stranger wearing his face, a young man who earned his white coat at twenty but now carries a constant, low-grade tension, fully aware that violence can arrive without warning. On his morning rounds, the consequences of his caution accumulate. He avoids the trauma bay when the overhead lights flicker off, because the sudden silence in the corridor mimics the dead air of that valley. He takes the service stairs to reach his shift, refusing the elevator, because his heart hammers against his ribs with every step, leaving him gasping in the stairwell long after he reaches the fourth floor. When a code blue blares from Room 12, the muffled shouts and the thud of a stretcher hitting the floor send his pulse through his throat. He finds himself backing out of the hallway, telling the charge nurse he has a charting emergency, though the real reason is that his chest constricts and his vision tunnels. He has built a rhythm of retreat: leaving early when the shift gets loud, eating lunch alone in his car, declining the post-call debriefs that ask him to talk about the night. His colleagues notice the distance, the way he steps back when conversations turn animated, but Andre assumes they think he is weak. What frightens him most is the quiet certainty that he will lose control in a critical moment, that the man who saved lives has been replaced by someone who is perpetually bracing for impact. He finally walks into the campus behavioral health clinic because the breathing has started happening during his own procedures, a tightness in his throat that threatens to paralyze him mid-suture. He does not want to lose his license, but he is more afraid of waking up one day and realizing he no longer recognizes the man who wakes in his empty apartment. He hopes someone can help him remember who he was before the silence, and teach him how to finally take a full breath again.
